hook_text: One grain of rice. Then two. Then four. The king laughed.
clip_script: Square one has one grain, which is two to the power zero. Square two has two, two to the power one. Square three has four, two squared. Square n has two to the power of n minus one. Square eleven has two to the power ten, one thousand and twenty-four grains — about a cupful. Square twenty-one has two to the power twenty, which is just over a million grains, a few sacks. Square thirty-one has two to the power thirty, about a billion grains — a warehouse. Square forty-one has two to the power forty, about a trillion. By the sixty-fourth square the number is two to the power sixty-three, about nine times ten to the power eighteen grains, more rice than has been grown in the whole of human history.
visual_style: A chessboard filling with rice square by square, the pile growing from a grain to a cup to sacks to a warehouse; powers of two and ten ticking in the corner
call_to_action: Open the full session to solve real problems with powers and roots.
